unit.unitTitle: Rocks, Soils and the Rock Cycle
unit.unitOverview: The ground under your feet is not one material. It is rock of three different families, each made in a different way, with soil on top of it that came from the rock itself. This unit teaches you to tell the three families apart, shows how a fossil survives inside one of them, looks at what soil is actually made of, and then puts the whole thing in motion: rock is not permanent, and the same material has been used and reused for billions of years.

Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Know that rocks can be classified as metamorphic, igneous and sedimentary, and describe the identifying features of each type of rock.
Describe the way fossils can form in sedimentary rocks.
Know that there are different types of soils and they can be classified based on their clay, sand and organic content.
Know that soil composition can change, which can support, or hinder, plant growth.
Describe the rock cycle and the formation of metamorphic, igneous and sedimentary rocks in terms of solidification, erosion, sedimentation, burial, metamorphism and melting.

sourceDocuments: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6, topics on rocks, soils and the rock cycle

outcomes: Name the three families of rock and say how each one forms.
Identify a rock's family from features you can see.
Explain how a fossil forms, and why it is found in only one of the three families.
Describe what soil is made of and how it forms from rock.
Classify a soil by its clay, sand and organic content.
Explain how soil composition affects what will grow in it.
Describe the rock cycle and name the processes that move material round it.

concepts.title: Three Families of Rock
concepts.explanation:
Every rock on Earth belongs to one of three families, and which family it is depends entirely on HOW IT WAS MADE rather than on what it is made of.

IGNEOUS rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens. The word comes from the Latin for fire. If it cools slowly deep underground the crystals grow large and you can see them easily, which is granite. If it cools fast at the surface after a volcanic eruption the crystals have no time to grow and the rock looks almost smooth, which is basalt - the rock most of the Rift Valley's lava flows are made of. The tell for an igneous rock is interlocking crystals with no layers at all.

SEDIMENTARY rock forms from sediment: loose grains of sand, mud and broken shell carried by water and dropped in layers, usually on a seabed or riverbed. Over a very long time the layers are buried, squeezed and cemented into solid rock. Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary. The tell is LAYERS, and often grains you can see or rub off, and sometimes fossils.

METAMORPHIC rock is either of the other two changed by enormous heat and pressure without melting. The word means 'changed in form'. Limestone under pressure becomes marble; mudstone becomes slate, which splits into flat sheets and is why slate makes roof tiles. The tell is crystals like an igneous rock but arranged in bands or stripes, as though the rock has been squeezed in one direction.

So the three questions to ask a rock are: does it have layers, does it have interlocking crystals, and are those crystals banded.
concepts.example: Three samples on a desk. One is speckled with big grey and pink crystals and has no layers - granite, igneous, cooled slowly underground. One is pale, gritty and clearly striped in bands you could count - sandstone, sedimentary. One is dark, hard and splits into flat sheets - slate, metamorphic, once mud.

concepts.title: How a Fossil Survives
concepts.explanation:
A FOSSIL is the preserved remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, turned to stone inside a rock. Almost every fossil ever found is in SEDIMENTARY rock, and the reason is worth working out rather than remembering.

The usual sequence runs like this. An animal or plant dies and its body settles somewhere sediment is being laid down - a riverbed, a lakebed, the sea floor. The soft parts rot away quickly, so what is usually left is bone, shell or wood. More sediment settles on top, layer on layer, burying it deeper. Over a very long time, water carrying dissolved minerals seeps through, and those minerals slowly replace the original material, particle by particle, until what remains has the shape of the bone and the substance of rock. Later, the rock above may be worn away and the fossil is exposed at the surface, which is how they are found.

Now the reason it has to be sedimentary. An igneous rock was molten - nothing living survives being melted. A metamorphic rock has been through such heat and pressure that any fossil in it is crushed and destroyed. Only sedimentary rock forms gently enough, at low temperature, and by burying things, which is exactly what a fossil needs.

A fossil is not the animal. It is rock in the animal's shape, which is why a fossil bone is far heavier than a real one and cannot be broken and eaten by anything.

And fossils are almost always very old - millions of years, not hundreds - because the burying, the mineral replacement and the wearing away above all take a very long time.
concepts.example: A fossil shell is found part-way up a hillside far inland. Three things follow: the rock is sedimentary, that place was once under water, and the whole hillside was later lifted up - because the shell certainly did not climb.

concepts.title: What Soil Is Actually Made Of
concepts.explanation:
Soil looks like one brown substance and is in fact a mixture of four things, and the proportions decide almost everything about it.

The largest part is MINERAL GRAINS, and these came from rock. Rain, frost, roots and moving water break rock down into smaller and smaller pieces over a very long time - that is WEATHERING - and those pieces are the grit and dust in soil. The grains come in three sizes and the names matter: SAND grains are the largest and you can feel them as grit; SILT is finer; CLAY grains are the smallest of all and feel smooth and sticky when wet.

The second part is ORGANIC MATTER, also called humus: the dark, crumbly remains of dead leaves, roots and animals, broken down by the decomposers you met in the ecosystems unit. It is what makes good soil dark, and it holds both water and nutrients.

The third and fourth are AIR and WATER, in the gaps between the grains. Roots need both, which is why a soil packed hard with no gaps grows very little.

So a soil is classified by which grain size dominates and how much organic matter it holds. A SANDY soil is mostly large grains, so water runs straight through it - it drains well, dries fast and loses its nutrients quickly. A CLAY soil is mostly the finest grains, so the gaps are tiny: it holds water so well that it waterlogs, and it sets hard when dry. A LOAM is a mixture of all three sizes with plenty of organic matter, and it is what a farmer hopes for, because it holds enough water without drowning the roots.
concepts.example: Rub a pinch of damp soil between your finger and thumb. If it feels gritty and falls apart, it is sandy. If it smears smooth and you can roll it into a thread, it has a great deal of clay. If it feels slightly gritty, holds together and smells earthy, it is a loam - and the dark colour is the organic matter.

concepts.title: Why the Soil Decides the Crop
concepts.explanation:
Soil composition is not a detail. It decides what will grow, how much water a field needs, and whether a harvest fails - and it can be changed, which is why any of this is worth knowing.

A plant needs three things from its soil: water, nutrients, and air around its roots. Each soil type supplies these differently. SANDY soil has large gaps, so water drains away fast and carries dissolved nutrients with it; it is easy to dig and warms early, and it dries out and goes hungry. CLAY soil holds water and nutrients well and holds them too well: the gaps are so small that water fills them all and the roots have no air, which drowns them, and in dry weather it bakes into a hard crust seedlings cannot push through. LOAM does both jobs adequately, which is why it grows most things.

And composition changes, in both directions. It gets WORSE when heavy rain washes the fine particles and nutrients away, when the same crop is grown year after year and takes the same nutrients out each time, or when the soil is left bare and the wind removes the top layer - the richest one. It gets BETTER when organic matter is put back: compost, manure or the remains of a previous crop dug in. Organic matter helps both problem soils, and it is the same substance either way - it opens up a clay soil so air and water can move, and it binds a sandy one so it holds water instead of losing it.

So the farmer's question is never just 'is this good soil'. It is 'what is this soil short of, and what would put it back'.
concepts.example: Two fields of maize a kilometre apart get the same rain. One is on sandy soil and the plants are short and yellowing, because the nutrients washed through weeks ago. The other has had manure dug in for years and the maize is tall and dark green. Same rain, same seed, different soil - and the difference was made, not found.

concepts.title: The Rock Cycle
concepts.explanation:
The three rock families are not three separate things that happen once. Each one can become either of the others, over and over, and the whole set of routes is called the ROCK CYCLE. Once you can see it as a cycle, rock stops being permanent.

Start with molten rock. It COOLS and SOLIDIFIES into igneous rock - fast at the surface, slowly underground.

Exposed at the surface, any rock is attacked. WEATHERING breaks it into loose grains; EROSION carries those grains away in rivers, wind and ice. They are TRANSPORTED and then DEPOSITED in layers somewhere lower down, usually under water. Buried, squeezed and cemented - COMPACTION and CEMENTATION - the layers become sedimentary rock.

Bury any rock deep enough and it meets great HEAT AND PRESSURE, which changes it without melting it into metamorphic rock.

Bury it deeper or hotter still and it MELTS, becoming molten rock again - and the cycle closes.

Every step can be skipped or repeated. A sedimentary rock can be weathered straight back into sediment without ever becoming metamorphic. An igneous rock can be metamorphosed and then melted. There is no fixed order and no starting point, which is why it is drawn as a circle with arrows both ways.

The time involved is the hardest part to hold. A single trip round takes many millions of years, and the atoms in a pebble you pick up today have very probably been through it several times, in rocks that no longer exist.
concepts.example: A grain of sand on a beach was once part of a granite mountain. Weathering freed it, a river carried it to the sea, and it will be buried and cemented into sandstone. If that sandstone is later pushed deep under a mountain range it will become quartzite, and if it goes deeper still it will melt - and one day cool as granite again.

explorations.title: Which Family Is This Rock?
explorations.context: To classify rocks by observable features rather than by guessing from colour.
explorations.prompt: Collect six different stones. For each, answer three questions in writing: does it have layers, does it have interlocking crystals, are the crystals in bands? Then name its family and say which feature decided it.
explorations.answer: Layers mean sedimentary; interlocking crystals with no layers mean igneous; crystals in bands or stripes mean metamorphic. Colour decides nothing - granite comes in several colours and so does sandstone.
explorations.hint: Wet each stone and look at it in good light. Layers and crystals both show up far better damp than dry.
explorations.explanation: Three Families of Rock: which family a rock belongs to is decided by how it formed, and each way of forming leaves a different visible mark.

explorations.title: What Is in This Soil?
explorations.context: To separate a soil sample into its parts and judge its composition.
explorations.prompt: Half-fill a clear jar with soil, top it up with water, screw the lid on and shake hard. Stand it somewhere still for a day, then describe the layers from the bottom up and estimate the share of each.
explorations.answer: Sand settles first at the bottom, then silt, then clay on top, with organic matter floating and water above. The thickness of each band gives you the soil's composition, and a thick clay band explains poor drainage.
explorations.hint: Leave it a full day - the clay is so fine that it is still settling hours later, and a reading taken too early makes the soil look sandier than it is.
explorations.explanation: What Soil Is Actually Made Of: soil is a mixture of mineral grains of three sizes, organic matter, air and water, and the proportions decide how it behaves.

explorations.title: Which Soil Holds Water?
explorations.context: To measure how differently two soils drain, and link it to what would grow in them.
explorations.prompt: Put equal amounts of sandy soil and clay soil in two funnels lined with filter paper. Pour the same amount of water through each and measure what comes out the bottom in two minutes. Predict first.
explorations.answer: Far more water runs straight through the sandy soil, because its gaps are large. The clay soil holds most of it back, which is why clay waterlogs and sand dries out.
explorations.hint: Pack both soils to the same firmness, or you will be testing your packing instead of the soil.
explorations.explanation: Why the Soil Decides the Crop: grain size sets the gap size, gap size sets the drainage, and drainage decides whether roots get water or drown.

methods.title: Classifying a Rock
methods.example: To decide which of the three families a rock belongs to, using what you can see.
steps: Wet the rock and look at it in good light.
Ask: can you see layers or bands of different material? If yes, it is sedimentary.
If not, ask: can you see crystals locked together? If yes, it is igneous or metamorphic.
Ask: are those crystals lined up in stripes? Stripes mean metamorphic; no pattern means igneous.
Try rubbing it: if grains come off on your fingers, that is more evidence for sedimentary.
Write down which feature decided your answer, not just the answer.

methods.title: The Jar Test for Soil
methods.example: To find the proportions of sand, silt and clay in a soil sample.
steps: Half-fill a straight-sided clear jar with soil and top it up with water.
Seal it and shake hard for a full minute, until no lumps remain.
Stand it somewhere it will not be knocked and leave it for 24 hours.
Measure the depth of each band: sand at the bottom, then silt, then clay.
Work out each band as a share of the total, and name the soil type.
Note any floating material - that is the organic matter.

methods.title: Tracing a Route Round the Rock Cycle
methods.example: To describe how one rock could become another, naming every process on the way.
steps: Write down the rock you are starting with and its family.
Write down the rock you are ending with and its family.
List the processes needed, in order, from weathering, erosion, transport, deposition, compaction, cementation, heat and pressure, melting, cooling and solidifying.
Check each step actually leads to the next - you cannot cement something that has not been deposited.
Say roughly how long the route would take, and where on Earth each step happens.

workedExamples.title: Naming a rock from its look
workedExamples.prompt: A rock is pale, feels gritty, and has clear horizontal stripes of slightly different colours. Which family, and how do you know?
workedExamples.solution: Sedimentary. The stripes are layers of sediment laid down one after another, and the grittiness is the individual grains. Neither igneous nor metamorphic rock is made of loose grains you can feel, and igneous rock has no layers at all.

workedExamples.title: Why no fossils in granite
workedExamples.prompt: Explain why a fossil is never found in granite.
workedExamples.solution: Granite is igneous, which means it formed from molten rock. Nothing living survives being melted, so there is nothing left to preserve. Fossils need a rock that forms gently and by burying things, and that is sedimentary rock - laid down cold, in layers, on a riverbed or seabed.

workedExamples.title: Advising a farmer with clay soil
workedExamples.prompt: A farmer's field waterlogs in the rains and bakes hard in the dry season. What is the soil, and what would you advise?
workedExamples.solution: It is a clay soil: the grains are so fine that the gaps are tiny, which holds water in the rains and sets solid when dry. Digging in organic matter - compost, manure or crop remains - opens the soil so air and water can move through it. The same addition would help a sandy soil, for the opposite reason: there it binds the soil so it holds water instead of losing it.

workedExamples.title: From mountain to sandstone and back
workedExamples.prompt: Describe how granite in a mountain could become granite again, naming every process.
workedExamples.solution: Weathering breaks the granite into grains; erosion and transport carry them down a river; deposition lays them in layers on a seabed; compaction and cementation make sandstone. Buried deeper, heat and pressure turn it into quartzite - metamorphic. Deeper or hotter still it melts, and cooling and solidifying make it igneous granite once more. Many millions of years for one lap.

practice.prompt: Name the three families of rock.
practice.hint: One is made by fire, one by layers, one by change.

practice.answer: Molten rock cools and solidifies - fast at the surface, slowly underground.
practice.hint: The name comes from the Latin for fire.

practice.prompt: What visible feature tells you a rock is sedimentary?
practice.answer: Layers, and often grains you can see or feel.
practice.hint: It was laid down a bit at a time.

practice.prompt: In which family of rock are fossils found, and why only that one?
practice.answer: Sedimentary. It forms gently, at low temperature, by burying things - igneous rock was molten and metamorphic rock has been crushed by heat and pressure, and neither leaves a fossil intact.
practice.hint: Ask what would happen to a bone in each of the three processes.

practice.prompt: Name the four things soil is made of.
practice.answer: Mineral grains from weathered rock, organic matter (humus), air and water.
practice.hint: Two of them are in the gaps rather than being solid.

practice.prompt: Put sand, silt and clay in order from largest grain to smallest.
practice.hint: The one you can feel as grit is the biggest.

practice.prompt: Why does water run straight through a sandy soil?
practice.answer: Its grains are large, so the gaps between them are large and water passes through easily - carrying dissolved nutrients with it.

practice.prompt: Digging in compost helps both a clay soil and a sandy one. Explain how one substance helps two opposite problems.
practice.answer: Organic matter opens a clay soil so air and water can move through it, and binds a sandy soil so it holds water instead of losing it. It improves the structure either way.
practice.hint: The two soils have opposite faults, and both faults are about the size of the gaps.

practice.prompt: Name the processes that turn loose sediment into sedimentary rock.
practice.answer: Deposition lays it down in layers, then compaction squeezes it and cementation glues the grains together.

practice.prompt: A fossil sea shell is found high up a hill far from the sea. What three things does that tell you?
practice.answer: The rock is sedimentary, that place was once under water, and the land has since been lifted up.
practice.hint: The shell did not travel there by itself.

activities.title: The rock family sort
activities.materials: Six or more different stones from around where you live, water, and a bright light.
steps: Wet each stone and look at it carefully in good light.
For each, write yes or no to: layers? interlocking crystals? crystals in bands?
Use your three answers to name the family, and write down which answer decided it.
Put any stone you could not decide about in a separate pile and say what made it hard.

activities.title: The soil jar
activities.materials: A straight-sided clear jar with a lid, a trowel of soil, water, a ruler.
steps: Half-fill the jar with soil, top up with water, seal and shake hard for a minute.
Stand it somewhere still and leave it a full day.
Measure the depth of each band from the bottom and work out each as a share of the total.
Name your soil type, and say one crop that would do well in it and one that would struggle.

activities.title: Draw the cycle and walk a route
activities.materials: A large sheet of paper and coloured pencils.
steps: Draw the three rock families in a triangle, with molten rock in the middle.
Draw and label an arrow for every process that leads from one to another.
Trace one complete route with your finger and say each process aloud in order.
Now trace a DIFFERENT route between the same two rocks, to show there is no fixed order.

rules.text: A rock's family is decided by HOW it formed, not by its colour.
Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the other two destroy them.
Grain size sets gap size, gap size sets drainage.
Any rock can become any other. The rock cycle has no starting point and no fixed order.

terms: Igneous
Rock formed when molten rock cooled and solidified.
Sedimentary
Rock formed from layers of sediment, compacted and cemented.
Metamorphic
Rock changed by great heat and pressure without melting.
Fossil
The preserved remains or trace of a living thing, turned to stone.
Weathering
The breaking down of rock in place, by rain, frost, roots and heat.
Erosion
The carrying away of broken rock by water, wind or ice.
Deposition
The laying down of transported sediment in layers.
Compaction
The squeezing of buried sediment by the weight above it.
Cementation
The gluing together of sediment grains by dissolved minerals.
Humus
The dark crumbly organic matter in soil, from decayed plants and animals.
Clay
The smallest mineral grains in soil; smooth, sticky, and holds water.
Sand
The largest mineral grains in soil; gritty, and drains fast.
Loam
A soil mixing sand, silt and clay with plenty of organic matter.
Rock cycle
The set of routes by which any rock family can become any other.
commonMistakes: A rock's family can be told from its colour.
It cannot. Granite comes in grey, pink and near-black, and so does sandstone. Layers, crystals and banding are the features that decide it.
Fossils can be found in any rock.
Almost only in sedimentary rock. Igneous rock was molten and metamorphic rock has been crushed, and neither leaves a fossil intact.
It is rock in the bone's shape. The original material was replaced, particle by particle, by minerals carried in water.
Mineral grains are the largest part, and soil is also organic matter, air and water - and it is the organic matter that makes it fertile.
Every rock is on its way to becoming another one. A single lap of the rock cycle takes millions of years, which is why it looks permanent.

connections.text: Digging in manure changes a soil's structure, which changes what it will grow - the science is the reason it works.
Slate roofs exist because a metamorphic rock splits into flat sheets, and granite kerbs because an igneous rock is hard and has no layers to split along.
The dark basalt of the lava flows is igneous rock that cooled fast at the surface, which is why its crystals are too small to see.
The jar test turns 'this soil feels heavy' into three numbers you can compare with somebody else's field.

fluency.prompt: In which family of rock are fossils found, and why only that one?
fluency.answer: Sedimentary. It forms gently, at low temperature, by burying things - igneous rock was molten and metamorphic rock has been crushed by heat and pressure, and neither leaves a fossil intact.
fluency.hint: Ask what would happen to a bone in each of the three processes.
fluency.errorFeedback: Sedimentary. It forms gently, at low temperature, by burying things - igneous rock was molten and metamorphic rock has been crushed by heat and pressure, and neither leaves a fossil intact.

fluency.prompt: Name the four things soil is made of.
fluency.answer: Mineral grains from weathered rock, organic matter (humus), air and water.
fluency.hint: Two of them are in the gaps rather than being solid.
fluency.errorFeedback: Mineral grains from weathered rock, organic matter (humus), air and water.

fluency.prompt: Put sand, silt and clay in order from largest grain to smallest.
fluency.hint: The one you can feel as grit is the biggest.

fluency.prompt: Why does water run straight through a sandy soil?
fluency.answer: Its grains are large, so the gaps between them are large and water passes through easily - carrying dissolved nutrients with it.
fluency.errorFeedback: Its grains are large, so the gaps between them are large and water passes through easily - carrying dissolved nutrients with it.

fluency.prompt: Digging in compost helps both a clay soil and a sandy one. Explain how one substance helps two opposite problems.
fluency.answer: Organic matter opens a clay soil so air and water can move through it, and binds a sandy soil so it holds water instead of losing it. It improves the structure either way.
fluency.hint: The two soils have opposite faults, and both faults are about the size of the gaps.
fluency.errorFeedback: Organic matter opens a clay soil so air and water can move through it, and binds a sandy soil so it holds water instead of losing it. It improves the structure either way.

fluency.prompt: Name the processes that turn loose sediment into sedimentary rock.
fluency.answer: Deposition lays it down in layers, then compaction squeezes it and cementation glues the grains together.
fluency.errorFeedback: Deposition lays it down in layers, then compaction squeezes it and cementation glues the grains together.

fluency.prompt: A fossil sea shell is found high up a hill far from the sea. What three things does that tell you?
fluency.answer: The rock is sedimentary, that place was once under water, and the land has since been lifted up.
fluency.hint: The shell did not travel there by itself.
fluency.errorFeedback: The rock is sedimentary, that place was once under water, and the land has since been lifted up.

realProblems.context: A gardener's vegetable bed floods after every rain and the seedlings rot.
realProblems.prompt: What is the likely soil type, and what would you advise?
realProblems.answer: A clay soil - the grains are so fine that water fills every gap and the roots get no air. Digging in plenty of organic matter would open the structure so water can drain and air can reach the roots.
realProblems.hint: Rotting roots is a sign of too little air, not too little water.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Clay holds water too well; organic matter dug in opens the gaps so the bed can drain.

realProblems.context: A builder digging a foundation finds a layer of rock full of shell fossils, with hard crystalline rock beneath it.
realProblems.prompt: What can you say about each layer, and which is older?
realProblems.answer: The fossil layer is sedimentary and was laid down under water. The crystalline layer below has no fossils and is igneous or metamorphic. The lower layer is older, because sediment is laid down on top of what is already there.
realProblems.hint: In undisturbed layers, deeper means older.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Fossils mean sedimentary and water; the crystalline rock beneath is older, because layers pile up from the bottom.

realProblems.context: Someone argues that quarrying is harmless because 'the rock will just grow back'.
realProblems.prompt: Use the rock cycle to answer them properly - what is right and what is wrong in that claim?
realProblems.answer: The cycle is real, so the material is not destroyed and will eventually become rock again. What is wrong is the timescale: one lap takes many millions of years, so nothing grows back on any human scale. The material is recycled; the rock, the hillside and the habitat are not replaced.
realProblems.hint: Agree with the part that is true before correcting the part that is not.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The cycle does recycle the material, over millions of years - which is far too slow to replace a quarried hillside in any useful sense.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why fossils are found in sedimentary rock and almost never in the other two families.
keyIdeas: Sedimentary rock forms gently, by burying
Metamorphic rock has been crushed by heat and pressure
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A fossil needs its remains buried gently and left undisturbed, and that is exactly how sedimentary rock forms: sediment settles in layers over the body, cold, and slowly cements around it. Igneous rock formed from molten rock, and nothing living survives melting. Metamorphic rock has been through such heat and pressure that any fossil in it is crushed out of shape. Only one of the three processes is gentle enough.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Organic matter improves both clay soil and sandy soil, although their problems are opposite. Explain how.
keyIdeas: Clay has gaps too small, sand too large
It opens clay and binds sand
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The two soils fail in opposite directions and for the same underlying reason - the size of the gaps between their grains. Clay's gaps are so small that water fills them all and roots get no air; sand's are so large that water runs straight through and takes the nutrients with it. Organic matter changes the structure rather than the grains: it opens a clay soil so water and air can move, and it binds a sandy one so it holds water. One substance, two opposite faults, because both faults are about structure.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is the rock cycle drawn as a circle with arrows both ways, rather than as a list of stages in order?
keyIdeas: Any family can become any other
Steps can be skipped or repeated
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because there is no fixed order. A sedimentary rock can be weathered straight back into sediment without ever becoming metamorphic; an igneous rock can be changed by pressure and then melted; the same material can go round several times. A list would imply a beginning and an end, and the cycle has neither - which is the whole point, because it means the rock under your feet is made of material that has been something else before.
